doc.title: Ed Polcer interviewed by Monk Rowe, Tarrytown, New York, October 31, 1998

title: Running Eddie Condon's club with no cover charge
summary: He loved running Condon's, with its musician-friendly drink prices, visitors like Basie band members, Joe Williams and Sinatra, and a ten-year run.

story.theme_name: Coming to New York: clubs, jams, and making it
story.community_name: Making it in New York: arrival, clubs and the scene

blocks.x: So you got into the Condon — picked up that Condon mantle or whatever it was. Did you enjoy your stint as a club owner?

Oh yeah. It was fantastic. I mean being in a center of my jazz world, owning, playing, band leading, managing and owning a club that represented everything I wanted to say, we didn’t have a cover charge, never had a music charge because when I grew up and © Fillius Jazz Archive -9-

coming to New York I was able to go into jazz clubs and plunk myself down at the Metropole, order one beer and sit for three hours and listen to the greatest music possible. So in the face of all these stiff music charges that had been put on all the clubs in New York to quote pay for the music it’s made it become more elitist so that the average person can’t come in and listen to it and be influenced by the music. So we presented a club there, up to the end we charged any musician who could prove he was a musician, if we didn’t know him and he had a union card, he could sit at the bar and drink for a buck and a quarter a drink. We finally upped it to a dollar and a half because some of the guys would come in and order a double Remy Martin and there it is, you got it baby, for a dollar and a half. But musicians came into the club. I mean there were nights where half of the Count Basie band was in there. They had finished a concert elsewhere. They’d come in. Joe Williams would come in and sing with us. He’d come in and the minute he’d come in we’d go into “Rosetta” and he’d [scats] he’d come walking up from the bar and sing. Frank Sinatra. All kinds of people came into that club. It was an exciting place to be for ten years. At the end for me, the administrative part of it and the drudgery of taking inventory of liquor and all that and food and closing up night after night and things, it was physically taxing. It was a glorious ten years though in New York. People would come from all over the world to Eddie Condon’s. If it wasn’t THE premier club it was one of three worldwide premier jazz clubs. It wasn’t any great, lavish place. It was just a jazz joint. It was a saloon, which is what Condon called his place, was a saloon. We served food, decent, a minimal amount of food but it was there. You’d come in. Our philosophy was you didn’t have to have a cover charge. If you liked it you’d stay and you’d order another drink. And by the time you’re through you’d probably spend the same amount of money that — you didn’t have to make a commitment. We advertised in all the local hotels, “music right around the corner” there was no fear of having to get in a cab, walk around New York they could walk two blocks and come to Eddie Condon’s and walk back to their hotel. So we had a worldwide, we had our own world wide web right there at Eddie Condon’s. It was great. It was glorious.
